about.title: About
additive.activated-charcoal.benefits: Deep black colorant with a draw-out feel — the signature of “detox” bars.
additive.activated-charcoal.cautions: Powder is messy and stains clothes/counters — wear a mask when handling the dust. Can mute other colors.
additive.activated-charcoal.name: Activated Charcoal
additive.activated-charcoal.water: Sift into a little oil and disperse before adding to avoid black clumps.
additive.activated-charcoal.wiki: Activated charcoal turns soap a true, dramatic black and is the classic detox-bar additive. It is very concentrated: a quarter to one teaspoon per pound of oils is plenty. Always sift it into a little oil or water and stir into a smooth slurry before adding at trace — otherwise you get stubborn black clumps. It can mute bright colors and gray out pastels, so design accordingly. Handle the fine powder carefully; it stains.
additive.bentonite.benefits: Draw-out, “detox” feel with a creamy lather — a favorite in oily-skin and mud-style bars.
additive.bentonite.cautions: Strongly absorbing; can be drying at higher rates. Slightly dulls fragrance. Gray-green tint unless white-bentonite grade is used.
additive.bentonite.name: Bentonite Clay
additive.bentonite.water: Absorbs more water than kaolin — always disperse in liquid first; batter thickens noticeably.
additive.bentonite.wiki: Bentonite is a swelling clay famous for drawing oils and impurities from skin. In cold-process soap it adds a creamy, dense lather and a slightly “clean” feel that oily-skin users love. It is one of the most water-hungry additives — dissolve it in a little water or oil before adding, and expect the batter to thicken. Keep it modest (0.5–3% of oils) so the bar does not become drying, and note that bentonite can mute fragrance oils.
additive.calendula.benefits: Traditional soothing herb — lovely orange-gold flecks in the bar.
additive.calendula.cautions: Petals can morph greenish in high-pH batter; test for exact color.
additive.calendula.name: Calendula Petals
additive.calendula.wiki: Calendula (marigold) petals are a centuries-old skin-soothing herb and a beautiful addition to soap — tiny orange-gold flecks scattered through the bar. Stir 1–2 tsp per pound of oils at trace, or sprinkle on top. Like many botanicals, the petals can shift color (often toward green or brown) in the lye environment, so test a small batch if the look matters.
additive.citric-acid.benefits: Chelating agent: binds minerals in hard water so your soap makes rich, creamy lather instead of soap scum — also helps prevent rancidity and brightens the bar.
additive.citric-acid.cautions: Never add citric acid to the lye solution — it fizzes violently. Dissolve it in the water first, then add the lye.
additive.citric-acid.lye: Citric acid neutralizes lye: every 1 g of citric acid consumes ~0.624 g NaOH (0.88 g pure KOH ≈ 0.978 g of 90% KOH). This calculator adds that extra lye automatically.
additive.citric-acid.name: Citric Acid
additive.citric-acid.phase: Dissolved in water BEFORE the lye
additive.citric-acid.wiki: Citric acid is the pro move for hard-water areas: it chelates (binds) calcium and magnesium so they cannot form soap scum, which means richer lather, cleaner rinsing, and less “bathtub ring.” Use 1–2% of oil weight. Critical rule: dissolve the citric acid in the water phase first, then add the lye — dropping it into lye solution fizzes and splashes dangerously. And because citric acid consumes lye, you must add compensating lye: 0.624 g NaOH per gram of citric acid (0.88 g KOH). This calculator does that math for you automatically and tells you the adjusted amount.
additive.coffee-grounds.benefits: Real exfoliation with a speckled look and a hint of coffee scent — the classic morning-scrub bar.
additive.coffee-grounds.cautions: Coarse grounds feel sharp — grind fine. Grounds can clog drains; use a tub drain screen.
additive.coffee-grounds.name: Used Coffee Grounds
additive.coffee-grounds.phase: At trace (or pressed into the top)
additive.coffee-grounds.wiki: Used coffee grounds are the classic exfoliating additive: they scrub, leave a charming speckle, and carry a faint coffee aroma. Dry and finely grind them before use — coarse bits feel like gravel in the shower. Add 1–2 tbsp per pound of oils at trace, or press grounds into the top of the loaf for a decorative scrub layer. Note that grounds in the batter can darken it slightly.
additive.colloidal-oats.benefits: Gentle exfoliation plus soothing skin feel — beta-glucan in oats calms itchy, dry, or sensitive skin and leaves a creamy, soft bar.
additive.colloidal-oats.cautions: Must be very finely ground — coarse oatmeal feels scratchy in the shower. Above ~5% the bar can soften and the batter thickens.
additive.colloidal-oats.name: Ground Oats (colloidal)
additive.colloidal-oats.water: Fine oats absorb water and thicken trace — add at light trace and stir, or disperse in a little oil first.
additive.colloidal-oats.wiki: Colloidal (finely ground) oatmeal is one of the gentlest additives in cold-process soap. The beta-glucan and avenanthramides are soothing and anti-inflammatory, which is why oats appear in sensitive-skin and eczema-friendly bars. Grind rolled oats to a powder in a blender (sift if needed) before adding. Keep to about 1–4% of oils so the bar stays smooth and hard. Sprinkle a little on top of the loaf instead for a decorative finish with zero scratchiness.
additive.french-green.benefits: Gentle detox with a soft sage-green tint — good for oily and combination skin bars.
additive.french-green.cautions: Green color can shift in high-pH batter; test your batch.
additive.french-green.name: French Green Clay (illite)
additive.french-green.water: Disperse in oil or water first; thickens trace like other clays.
additive.french-green.wiki: French green clay (illite) is a classic spa clay with a beautiful natural green color. It gently absorbs excess oil, which makes it popular in facial and oily-skin bars. The green comes from iron oxides and decomposed plant matter, and it can morph slightly in the high-pH lye environment — test a small batch if the exact shade matters. Use 1–2 tsp per pound of oils, added at trace.
additive.goat-milk-powder.benefits: Creamy, gentle bar with a soft lotion feel — lactic acid in milk is naturally mild on skin.
additive.goat-milk-powder.cautions: Milk can scorch or turn orange/brown if the lye solution overheats — keep it cool and add lye slowly. Adds a faint sweet-milk scent.
additive.goat-milk-powder.name: Goat Milk Powder
additive.goat-milk-powder.phase: Dissolved in water before lye (or at trace)
additive.goat-milk-powder.water: Dissolve powder in the water first; some makers freeze the milk and add lye slowly to avoid heat.
additive.goat-milk-powder.wiki: Goat milk makes famously creamy, gentle bars — the lactic acid and fats in milk soften skin, and the finished bar feels luxurious. Powdered goat milk is the easy route: dissolve it in your water phase before adding lye, and keep the solution cool so the milk does not scorch (the classic trick is freezing the milk and adding lye slowly). Typical use is about 1 tbsp per pound of oils. The bar may have a subtle milky scent and a slightly creamier color.
additive.honey.benefits: Humectant that draws moisture to skin, boosts bubbles, and adds a subtle golden tint and mild scent.
additive.honey.cautions: Honey + lye heat up — it can push the batch into gel fast or even overheat in the mold (“soap volcano”). Start at 1 tsp PPO.
additive.honey.name: Honey
additive.honey.water: Dissolve honey in a little warm water (not lye) before adding to avoid clumps.
additive.honey.wiki: Honey is a natural humectant: it pulls moisture into the skin, and soapmakers love the extra bubbles and golden glow it gives a bar. The catch is temperature — honey makes the batter heat up, so a high-honey batch can gel aggressively or overflow the mold. Start conservative (1 tsp per pound of oils), add at trace dissolved in a little warm water, and keep an eye on the mold. Many makers pair honey with oats or milk for a classic “breakfast” bar.
additive.kaolin.benefits: Silky, slippery bar with a smooth glide. Gentle for sensitive skin, reduces the “drag” of a plain bar, and helps lighten or brighten colors.
additive.kaolin.cautions: None significant at normal rates; over 3–4% it can mute lather and slightly dry skin.
additive.kaolin.name: Kaolin Clay
additive.kaolin.water: Clays absorb water and thicken batter — disperse in a little oil or water before adding, or blend at light trace.
additive.kaolin.wiki: Kaolin is the gentlest clay — a fine white powder that gives soap a silky, cosmetic feel. It is popular in facial and sensitive-skin bars because it is very mild and adds slip without pulling moisture. Because it absorbs oils and water, disperse it in a little liquid or oil first and add at light trace. Kaolin also brightens colors and can be used to matte or lighten a design. Typical use is 1–2 tsp per pound of oils.
additive.lavender-buds.benefits: Pretty botanical decoration with light exfoliation and a whisper of lavender.
additive.lavender-buds.cautions: Buds can turn brown or bleed color in the batter; sharp edges may irritate — crush lightly or use on top only.
additive.lavender-buds.name: Lavender Buds
additive.lavender-buds.wiki: Lavender buds are the prettiest botanical garnish: sprinkle them on top of the loaf for a rustic look, or stir them in for gentle exfoliation. In the batter they can darken to brown over time, so many makers press buds only into the top. Use 1–2 tsp per pound of oils and crush them lightly if you want them less prickly.
additive.mica.benefits: Shimmer, pearl, and vivid colors — the modern soapmaker’s palette.
additive.mica.cautions: Only use cosmetic/skin-safe mica (never craft-store mica). Some colors morph or migrate; test.
additive.mica.name: Skin-safe Mica
additive.mica.water: Disperse in a little oil to avoid streaks and speckles.
additive.mica.wiki: Micah is a mineral pigment ground with oxides for color — the workhorse of modern soap design. A tiny amount (⅛–1 tsp per pound of oils) gives shimmer or solid color. Always buy mica labeled safe for cosmetics: some craft micas contain pigments not approved for skin. Color shift is batch-specific — reds and oranges can morph in lye — so test before committing a full batch.
additive.pink-clay.benefits: Soft blush-pink tint with kaolin’s gentle, silky feel.
additive.pink-clay.cautions: Natural pink can fade or shift in lye; test.
additive.pink-clay.name: Pink Clay (kaolin + iron oxide)
additive.pink-clay.wiki: Pink clay is mostly kaolin tinted with natural iron oxides. It gives soap a soft rose or blush color while keeping kaolin’s mild, silky character — a lovely choice for floral or romantic bars. Use 1–2 tsp per pound of oils at trace. The pink can lighten in the lye environment, so test a small batch for exact shade.
additive.poppy-seeds.benefits: Gentle, uniform exfoliation with a distinctive dotted look.
additive.poppy-seeds.cautions: Some find seeds slightly sharp; stir well or they sink unevenly.
additive.poppy-seeds.name: Poppy Seeds
additive.poppy-seeds.wiki: Poppy seeds give soap a gentle, even scrub and that signature polka-dot look. They are small and smooth enough for most skin. Use 1–2 tsp per pound of oils, stirred in at trace; they can settle, so give the batter a final mix right before pouring. For a softer scrub, grind them lightly first.
additive.rhassoul.benefits: Silky, slip-rich bar with real draw-out power — beloved for oily skin and a luxurious feel.
additive.rhassoul.cautions: Can be drying at high rates; adds a tan/brown tint.
additive.rhassoul.name: Rhassoul Clay (Moroccan)
additive.rhassoul.wiki: Rhassoul (ghassoul) clay from Morocco is prized for its high mineral content and exceptional silky slip. It draws out oils and impurities while leaving skin soft, and it adds a wonderfully smooth feel to bars. Its tan color can warm up a design. Standard use is 1–2 tsp per pound of oils, added at trace after dispersing in a little oil or water.
additive.rosemary-extract.benefits: Natural antioxidant that slows rancidity (DOS) and extends shelf life — cheap insurance for high-iodine recipes.
additive.rosemary-extract.cautions: A tiny amount is all you need; too much can slightly discolor or scent the bar.
additive.rosemary-extract.name: Rosemary Oleoresin (ROE)
additive.rosemary-extract.phase: Added to the oils (or at trace)
additive.rosemary-extract.wiki: Rosemary oleoresin extract (ROE) is the natural soapmaker’s shelf-life insurance: it is a potent antioxidant that slows the oxidation (dreaded orange spots / DOS) that can attack high-oleic or high-iodine recipes. Add just a few drops — about ¼ tsp per pound of oils at most — to the warm oils before mixing, or stir in at trace. It is nearly invisible and tastes/smells like nothing in the finished bar.
additive.salt.benefits: Hardens the bar and produces a dense, creamy lather — the heart of classic brine and salt bars.
additive.salt.cautions: Accelerates trace strongly; can be drying at high rates. True salt bars run 25–50%+ salt with 20% superfat — a different style than this gentle range.
additive.salt.name: Salt (sea / table)
additive.salt.phase: Dissolved in water (brine) or at trace
additive.salt.water: Dissolve salt in the water phase before lye, or add at trace; undissolved crystals stay gritty.
additive.salt.wiki: Salt hardens soap and gives it that dense, creamy, almost lotion-like lather. At gentle rates (1–2 tbsp per pound of oils) it is a texture upgrade for any bar. True “salt bars” are a different beast: 25–50% salt and high superfat (often 20%), which this gentle range is not. Salt accelerates trace, so work quickly, and dissolve it in the water phase before adding lye to avoid a gritty bar.
additive.silk.benefits: Gives bars a silky, glossy, almost powdery skin feel — the protein sericin coats the bar surface.
additive.silk.cautions: Takes time to dissolve in lye water; a pinch goes a long way.
additive.silk.name: Silk Fibers (sericin)
additive.silk.water: Stir silk fibers into the water before the lye and give them time to dissolve completely.
additive.silk.wiki: Real silk fibers (or silk protein) add an unmistakable silky, smooth glide to soap — the sericin protein creates a soft, slightly glossy surface. You only need a pinch (about ¼ tsp per pound of oils): dissolve the fibers in the water phase before adding lye and let them break down fully. It is the classic “luxury bar” trick and costs almost nothing per batch.
additive.sodium-lactate.benefits: Hardens bars noticeably, speeds unmolding, and gives cleaner cuts — a lifesaver for high-soft-oil recipes.
additive.sodium-lactate.cautions: Can speed trace slightly; measure accurately.
additive.sodium-lactate.name: Sodium Lactate
additive.sodium-lactate.wiki: Sodium lactate is a liquid salt of lactic acid sold specifically for soapmaking. A teaspoon per pound of oils makes bars harder and easier to unmold and cut — the go-to fix for soft, slow-curing recipes heavy in olive or other conditioning oils. Add it to the cooled lye solution before mixing. It can slightly accelerate trace, so have your mold ready.
additive.spirulina.benefits: Vivid natural green colorant with trace minerals and a nutrient-rich story.
additive.spirulina.cautions: Green can morph grayish or blue-green in lye; expensive — use sparingly.
additive.spirulina.name: Spirulina Powder
additive.spirulina.wiki: Spirulina is a blue-green algae that gives soap a striking natural green. A quarter to one teaspoon per pound of oils is plenty. The color is a bit temperamental in high-pH batter — it can shift toward gray or blue-green depending on the recipe and cure — so test your batch. It adds trace minerals and a lovely “green beauty” angle to the label.
additive.sugar.benefits: Boosts rich, stable lather — especially helpful in high-oleic (castile-style) bars.
additive.sugar.cautions: Sugar in lye water heats up; dissolve in water before the lye or add to cooled lye water.
additive.sugar.name: Sugar (granulated)
additive.sugar.water: Do not pour sugar straight into hot lye — it can scorch and darken.
additive.sugar.wiki: Plain table sugar is a quiet workhorse additive: dissolved in the water phase it increases lather, giving castile and other high-oleic bars a much fluffier, more stable suds. Use about 1 tsp per pound of oils. Dissolve it in the water before you add the lye (or stir into cooled lye water) — dropping sugar into hot lye solution can scorch it and brown the batch.
additive.titanium-dioxide.benefits: Bright white colorant and opacifier — makes a clean white base for vivid swirls.
additive.titanium-dioxide.cautions: Disperse in oil or glycerin first; it does not mix into water. Can be slightly drying at high rates.
additive.titanium-dioxide.name: Titanium Dioxide (TiO₂)
additive.titanium-dioxide.wiki: Titanium dioxide is the standard white pigment in soapmaking: it makes bars bright white and opaque, and it is the base for most pastel swirls. It must be dispersed in a little oil (or glycerin) into a smooth slurry before adding — dumped into water it just clumps. Use ¼–1 tsp per pound of oils. In the U.S. the FD&C-grade is generally regarded as safe for rinse-off cosmetics; buy from a soapmaking supplier.
additive.turmeric.benefits: Warm yellow-orange natural colorant with antioxidant curcumin — “golden milk” bars.
additive.turmeric.cautions: Can morph to orange or red-brown in lye; stains skin and cloths while wet.
additive.turmeric.name: Turmeric Powder
additive.turmeric.water: Disperse in a little oil first to avoid streaks.
additive.turmeric.wiki: Turmeric gives soap a sunny yellow-orange that deepens over time — in the lye environment it often shifts toward orange or terracotta, which is part of its charm. It also brings curcumin, a natural antioxidant. Use ¼–1 tsp per pound of oils, dispersed in oil first to avoid streaks, and remember it stains hands, towels, and molds while the batter is wet. Pair with a little white clay for a softer tone.

oil.apricot.name: Apricot Kernel Oil
oil.apricot.wiki: Similar niche to sweet almond — light conditioning and slip for facial or gentle body bars. Balance iodine with hard oils for shelf life. Soaping temp: liquid at room temp; works well at 90–115°F. Traces moderately — slightly faster than pure olive.
oil.argan.name: Argan Oil
oil.argan.wiki: Famous cosmetic oil. In soap, much of the hype is marketing — saponified argan won’t behave like leave-on serum — but small amounts add conditioning story and feel. Use 1–5% and save bulk budget for workhorse oils.
oil.avocado.name: Avocado Oil
oil.avocado.wiki: Rich, conditioning oil popular in facial and luxury bars. Penetrating feel; can discolor slightly green depending on grade. Use as a portion of your soft-oil phase rather than the sole base if you want faster hardness. Soaping temp: liquid at room temp; heat-stable up to ~130°F. Traces slowly — good for swirls. Unrefined (green) avocado can tint batter light green that fades to tan.
oil.babassu.name: Babassu Oil
oil.babassu.wiki: Coconut’s elegant cousin — lauric-rich, hard, bubbly, often described as slightly silkier. Use like coconut in the lauric budget. Popular in luxury and palm-free recipes as a coconut partial substitute. Soaping temp: solid below ~76°F — warm to 90–105°F. Slightly slower trace than coconut but still a fast mover.
oil.beeswax.name: Beeswax
oil.beeswax.wiki: Not a true oil — wax that hardens bars and can reduce lather if overdone. Typical soap use 1–3% (rarely above 5%). Also slows absorption of water into the bar. Soaping temp: melts ~145°F — must be melted into hot oils (150–160°F) before adding lye. Cool the oils+beeswax blend back to ~120°F before adding lye, or the wax will re-solidify on contact with cooler lye water. Traces fast once lye is in. Note: beeswax is common in candles too (see wax wiki).
oil.canola.name: Canola / Rapeseed
oil.canola.wiki: Budget-friendly soft oil. Makes conditioning but softer bars; often used to stretch olive in large batches. Not a lather star — lean on coconut/castor for bubbles. Slowish trace helps beginners.
oil.castor.name: Castor Oil
oil.castor.wiki: The lather amplifier. Ricinoleic acid is uniquely humectant and makes bubbles denser and longer-lasting. Typical use is 3–8%; above ~10% can make bars soft or sticky. Does not replace hard oils — it enhances whatever lather your formula already has.
oil.chicken-fat.name: Chicken Fat (Schmaltz)
oil.chicken-fat.wiki: Old-world soap fat that surprises newcomers — high oleic (~45%) and palmitic (~25%) give conditioning AND structure. Rendered schmaltz has a mild scent that vanishes in well-cured soap. Semi-solid at room temp, melts ~85–95°F. Soaping temp: warm to 100–115°F for smooth blending; strain rendered fat well — bits of skin or seasoning will spoil in the bar. Use 20–50% as a lard alternative. Naturally palm-free and often free from a butcher or kitchen scrap.
oil.cocoa.name: Cocoa Butter
oil.cocoa.wiki: Hard, silky butter that firms bars and adds a “expensive” glide. Natural chocolate scent in unrefined grades. Keep moderate (often 5–15%) — very high cocoa can make brittle bars. Excellent palm-free hardness helper alongside tallow or coconut. Soaping temp: melts ~94–98°F — warm oils to 105–120°F. Cocoa solidifies fast when batter cools; keep everything warm and move briskly. Unrefined cocoa has a stronger chocolate scent that can carry into the bar.
oil.coconut-fractionated.name: Fractionated Coconut
oil.coconut-fractionated.wiki: MCT / caprylic-capric fraction — liquid at room temp, very high SAP, strong cleansing. Different animal from solid 76° coconut. Use carefully; high SAP means more lye per gram. More common in liquid soap and light esters than classic bar bases.
oil.coconut.name: Coconut Oil
oil.coconut.wiki: King of fluffy bubbles and cleansing. Lauric and myristic acids give rock-hard bars and big lather — and can strip skin if overused. Most balanced recipes stay around 15–30% coconut (or total lauric oils). Higher % works for laundry or salt bars with extra superfat. Soaping temp: solid below 76°F — warm to 90–100°F to melt fully. Traces fast at any temp; work quickly once lye hits the oils. Cooler soaping (85–95°F) buys a little more swirl time.
oil.corn.name: Corn Oil
oil.corn.wiki: Frugal kitchen standby — high linoleic with moderate oleic. Liquid at room temp and stays liquid (pour point well below freezing). In soap: conditioning without much lather, much like soybean. Warm to ~100°F for even blending. High iodine means limit to ~15–25% for shelf life; pair with hard oils for structure. Soaping temp: room-temp to warm — corn oil is thin and easy to blend at any temp above ~50°F.
oil.crisco.name: Vegetable Shortening (Crisco)
oil.crisco.wiki: The classic blue tub — soy + fully-hydrogenated cottonseed (classic formula) or soy + palm (new formula). Behaves similarly to lard in soap: creamy lather, decent hardness, economical. Solid at room temp; melts ~115°F. Soaping temps: keep oils 100–120°F — too hot and it traces faster; too cool and the hydrogenated fraction can grain. Check your label: new-Crisco (palm) traces a touch slower than old-Crisco (cottonseed). Widely available palm-free option.
oil.cupuacu.name: Cupuacu Butter
oil.cupuacu.wiki: Amazonian soft butter with remarkable water-absorption capacity — can hold 4× its weight in water, which translates to a uniquely creamy, emollient bar. Oleic ~42%, stearic ~32% — softer than shea at room temp. Melts ~86–95°F. Soaping temp: melts easily at 95–110°F; its water hunger thickens trace, so blend at light trace and work quickly. Use 3–10% for luxury skin feel without heavy hardness. Lathers better than most butters at the same %.
oil.emu.name: Emu Oil
oil.emu.wiki: Penetrating animal oil (ratite family) with a fatty-acid profile close to human skin lipids — high oleic (~47%), palmitic (~22%), and unique terpenes. Liquid at room temp. Soaping temp: 95–110°F — heat degrades the bioactive terpenes, so keep it modest. Use 2–8% as a luxury conditioner; too much kills lather. Some soapers add it at trace (after cook in HP) to preserve the skin-feel actives. Not vegan; label clearly. Pairs with shea and kokum in premium therapeutic-style bars.
oil.evening-primrose.name: Evening Primrose Oil
oil.evening-primrose.wiki: Star facial-bar addition — rich in gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), prized for mature or sensitive skin. Very high iodine; delicate oil that oxidizes fast when heated. Soaping temp: critical to soap cool — keep oils 85–100°F max. Hot lye or gel phase destroys the GLA value. Use 3–8%, and hot-process soapers should add after cook. Store the raw oil in the fridge. Pairs well with balanced oleic bases.
oil.goose-fat.name: Goose Fat
oil.goose-fat.wiki: The connoisseur's rendered fat — higher oleic than lard (~56%) with enough palmitic (~22%) for a silky, long-lasting bar that rivals premium plant blends. Semi-solid at room temp; renders clear gold. Soaping temp: 100–115°F — clean-rendered fat soaps smoothly with a moderate trace. The bar cures to a creamy, dense lather with excellent conditioning. Use 20–50% in place of lard or tallow. Worth the effort of rendering if you roast goose.
oil.grapeseed.name: Grapeseed Oil
oil.grapeseed.wiki: Light, fast-absorbing oil. High linoleic content — use sparingly for shelf life. Nice silky feel in facial bars when balanced with stable oils and a solid cure. Soaping temp: liquid at room temp — keep oils 90–110°F. Heat-sensitive: high temps accelerate oxidation of the polyunsaturated fraction, so avoid gel phase if you want max shelf life.
oil.hazelnut.name: Hazelnut Oil
oil.hazelnut.wiki: Luxurious nut oil — high oleic (~78%) gives conditioning and a warm, faintly nutty scent that can survive saponification. Liquid at room temp. Soaping temp: 90–110°F — the natural scent is more pronounced when you soap cooler, fading somewhat at higher temps. Lovely at 5–15% in facial or gourmet bars. Pairs beautifully with cocoa butter and shea for a premium nut-butter bar.
oil.hemp.name: Hemp Seed Oil
oil.hemp.wiki: Nutrient-rich with a green hue and very high iodine — wonderful skin feel, shorter shelf life. Keep low (often 5–15%), consider rosemary oleoresin (ROE) antioxidant, and sell/use bars promptly. Soaping temp: highly heat-sensitive — soap cool (85–100°F) to preserve the omega profile. Refrigerate raw oil. Avoid gel phase; the green fades with heat and time.
oil.high-oleic-safflower.name: High-Oleic Safflower Oil
oil.high-oleic-safflower.wiki: The stable safflower — ~75% oleic vs regular safflower's ~14%. In soap this behaves more like a light olive than the high-linoleic DOS bomb. Liquid at room temp; thin and easy to blend. Soaping temp: any reasonable temp (90–130°F) — very forgiving. Mild conditioning with a gentle lather. Use 15–40% as a neutral soft-oil base. Always check the label: regular "safflower oil" is high-linoleic unless marked "high-oleic."
oil.high-oleic-sunflower.name: High-Oleic Sunflower Oil
oil.high-oleic-sunflower.wiki: The sunflower you WANT for soap — bred for high oleic (~82%) with very low linoleic, making it stable and olive-like without olive's slow cure. Liquid at room temp, thin and easy to work with. Soaping temp: room-temp to 120°F — remarkably forgiving. Traces slowly like olive, giving plenty of swirl time. Excellent 20–50% olive alternative in recipes where you want conditioning without months of cure. Check your bottle: regular (linoleic) sunflower is the DOS-prone one — high-oleic is the soaper's friend.
oil.illipe.name: Illipe Butter
oil.illipe.wiki: Borneo's answer to cocoa butter — exceptionally hard (stearic ~42%, palmitic ~15%, oleic ~38%). Adds firmness and a silky glide to luxury bars. Melts ~98–102°F. Soaping temp: melt into oils at 110–120°F; solidify risk if batter cools too much. Similar to cocoa butter in hardness but with slightly less brittleness. Use 5–15% for a firm, silky palm-free bar that lasts in the shower.
oil.jojoba.name: Jojoba Oil
oil.jojoba.wiki: Technically a liquid wax ester, not a triglyceride — very low SAP. Adds luxury slip and stability more than bulk saponified soap. Expensive; 1–5% as a superfat-adjacent conditioner is common. Doesn’t behave like olive as a primary oil.
oil.kokum.name: Kokum Butter
oil.kokum.wiki: India's gift to hard bars — very high stearic (~54%) with moderate oleic, making it one of the hardest plant butters. Non-greasy, matte feel; great for facial bars and palm-free hardness. Melts ~100–104°F — warmer than cocoa butter. Soaping temp: melt fully into warm oils (110–125°F) and blend well; kokum graining can happen if the batter cools below ~100°F. Use 5–20% for hardness without the brittleness of too much cocoa. Pairs with soft conditioning oils for a balanced premium bar.
oil.kukui.name: Kukui Nut Oil
oil.kukui.wiki: Hawaiian treasure — very high linoleic and linolenic for a fast-absorbing, conditioning bar. Liquid at room temp; highly unsaturated = short shelf life. Soaping temp: soaps best cool (85–100°F) to minimize oxidation and preserve the delicate fatty-acid profile. Keep raw oil refrigerated. Use 3–8% as a superfat-adjacent booster, not a bulk oil. Regional soapmakers love it for island-inspired bars.
oil.lard.name: Lard
oil.lard.wiki: Old-school soapmaking staple. Creamy lather, good hardness, excellent conditioning — often compared favorably to palm in palm-free bars. Mild scent when fresh and well-rendered. Fantastic everyday workhorse at 30–60%. Soaping temp: melts ~85–100°F — warm to 105–120°F. Well-rendered leaf lard is nearly odorless; lower grades may carry a faint scent. Traces moderately fast — not as fast as coconut, not as slow as olive.
oil.macadamia.name: Macadamia Oil
oil.macadamia.wiki: Silky luxury oil with palmitoleic acid (also found in sebum). Lovely skin feel; moderate iodine vs many seed oils. Excellent 5–15% “treat” oil in premium bars. Soaping temp: liquid at room temp; stable at normal soaping temps (95–120°F). Traces at a moderate pace — good middle ground for most recipes.
oil.mango.name: Mango Butter
oil.mango.wiki: Similar conditioning niche to shea with a lighter skin feel and little scent when refined. Good mid-range butter for silky bars without heavy cocoa firmness. Pairs well with olive and rice bran. Soaping temp: melts ~86–95°F — warm to 100–115°F. Traces slower than shea and cocoa, giving a longer working window for swirls.
oil.meadowfoam.name: Meadowfoam Oil
oil.meadowfoam.wiki: Remarkably stable specialty oil with long-chain fatty acids. Tiny amounts add conditioning and shelf help. Pricey — treat as a booster (2–8%), not a bulk oil.
oil.murumuru.name: Murumuru Butter
oil.murumuru.wiki: The hardest lauric butter — lauric ~46%, myristic ~28%, making it behave almost like solid coconut on steroids. Very high SAP means more lye per gram. Melts ~92–100°F. Soaping temp: 105–120°F to stay fully liquid; traces FAST due to the lauric-myristic punch — have your mold ready. Use 3–10%; a little goes a long way for hardness + bubbles. Too much and the bar can be drying — keep superfat healthy (>6%).
oil.neem.name: Neem Oil
oil.neem.wiki: Traditional Ayurvedic oil with a powerful garlic-sulfur aroma that softens but rarely vanishes in soap. Used in garden/skin-support folklore bars; keep low and pair with strong FO/EO blends if scent bothers you. Soaping temp: semi-solid below ~70°F — warm to 90–105°F to pour. The aroma is pungent when warm; ventilate well. Traces fast.
oil.olive.name: Olive Oil
oil.olive.wiki: The classic castile base. High oleic content makes a mild, conditioning bar that can take months to harden fully when used at 100%. Pure olive soaps are legendary for sensitive skin but need a long cure (often 6–12 months) for a firm bar. Speeds: slow trace — great for intricate swirls. Pair with a hard oil if you want everyday firmness sooner.
oil.palm-kernel.name: Palm Kernel Oil
oil.palm-kernel.wiki: Behaves more like coconut than soft palm oil — high lauric content, hard bar, bubbly lather. Count it toward your total lauric load with coconut and babassu. Excellent hardness booster in small amounts. Soaping temp: solid below ~80°F — warm to 90–105°F. Fast tracer like coconut; have your mold ready.
oil.palm.name: Palm Oil
oil.palm.wiki: Adds hardness and a creamy, stable lather without as much “strip” as coconut. Often 20–40% in traditional triple-oil bars (olive/coconut/palm). Choose RSPO or sustainable sources if palm ethics matter to you. Can be replaced with tallow, lard, or stearic-rich butters in palm-free formulas. Soaping temp: solid below ~95°F — warm oils to 100–120°F to fully melt. Palm graining (white specks) happens if batter cools too much; blend thoroughly and keep above 100°F.
oil.peanut.name: Peanut Oil
oil.peanut.wiki: Common deep-fry oil with a surprisingly nice soap profile: solid oleic backbone (~50%) plus ~30% linoleic gives conditioning with decent stability. Liquid at room temp. High smoke point means it tolerates warm soaping well — oils at 110–130°F work fine. MUST label for peanut allergy if selling. Use 10–25% in the soft-oil phase alongside olive or rice bran. Trace speed: moderate — slower than coconut, faster than pure olive.
oil.pumpkin-seed.name: Pumpkin Seed Oil
oil.pumpkin-seed.wiki: Dark green oil with natural vitamin E and phytosterols. In soap the green fades to tan/beige (the lye eats the chlorophyll), but conditioning stays. Liquid at room temp; high iodine — keep modest and cure well. Soaping temp: 90–110°F — the green hue is stronger at lower temps, but saponification bleaches it regardless. Use 5–15% for a skin-nourishing regional bar.
oil.rice-bran.name: Rice Bran Oil
oil.rice-bran.wiki: Excellent olive alternative: conditioning, creamy lather contribution, and natural antioxidants (gamma-oryzanol). Slightly faster than pure olive for usable hardness. Popular 20–50% in modern palm-free recipes.
oil.rosehip.name: Rosehip Seed Oil
oil.rosehip.wiki: The most delicate common soaping oil — extremely high linolenic acid (~40%) and very high iodine. Face-bar legend for its retinoid-like reputation (natural trans-retinoic acid precursors). Soaping temp: MUST soap cool — 85–95°F max; hot lye destroys the delicate actives. Keep raw oil in the fridge. Use 1–5% — treat it as a superfat additive, not a structural oil. Hot-process users should add after cook only.
oil.safflower.name: Safflower Oil
oil.safflower.wiki: Often very high-linoleic — soft bars and DOS risk if used heavily. High-oleic safflower is a better soaping choice when available. Keep percentages modest.
oil.sal.name: Sal Butter
oil.sal.wiki: Another Indian hard butter (Shorea robusta) — stearic ~44%, oleic ~40%. Slightly softer than kokum with a grainier raw texture that smooths in soap. Melts ~95–100°F. Soaping temp: melt into oils at 105–120°F and stir thoroughly — raw sal can be lumpy if not fully melted. Use 5–20% for hardness with a creamier feel than cocoa. Excellent palm-free choice alongside shea or mango.
oil.sesame.name: Sesame Oil
oil.sesame.wiki: Traditional oil with a distinctive nutty scent that can linger. Conditioning soft oil; not a primary lather source. Fun in themed or regional recipes at low–moderate %.
oil.shea.name: Shea Butter
oil.shea.wiki: Luxurious conditioning from unsaponifiables that survive saponification. Adds creaminess and skin feel; too much (often >25–30%) can mute lather and slow hardness. Refined shea is milder scented; unrefined has a nutty aroma some love. Great at 5–15% in everyday bars. Soaping temp: melts ~90–100°F — warm oils to 105–120°F. Shea can grain if the batter cools; stir thoroughly after adding lye. Unrefined shea traces faster than refined.
oil.soybean.name: Soybean Oil
oil.soybean.wiki: Common economical oil with higher iodine. Fine in moderation; large percentages soften bars and raise DOS risk. Many soapers prefer olive, rice bran, or high-oleic options for longevity.
oil.sunflower.name: Sunflower Oil
oil.sunflower.wiki: Affordable linoleic-rich oil. High iodine means softer bars and faster rancidity risk (DOS — dreaded orange spots) if overused. Prefer high-oleic sunflower when you can; keep total high-iodine oils in check and cure/store well.
oil.sweet-almond.name: Sweet Almond Oil
oil.sweet-almond.wiki: Light conditioning oil with excellent slip — favorite for massage-bar feel and gentle recipes. Higher iodine than olive, so balance with hard oils and don’t overload if shelf life is a concern.
oil.tallow.name: Beef Tallow
oil.tallow.wiki: The classic hard, white, long-lasting bar fat. Creamy lather and great cure hardness. Quality and scent depend on rendering; many soapers prefer grass-fed or carefully cleaned tallow. Cornerstone of traditional and palm-free formulas. Soaping temp: melts ~100–110°F — warm oils to 110–125°F. Tallow traces faster than lard; keep temps steady. Clean-rendered tallow has almost no scent in the finished bar.
oil.tamanu.name: Tamanu Oil
oil.tamanu.wiki: Thick, dark-green tropical oil revered in Pacific healing traditions. Unusually rich in resinous compounds and calophyllolide — some of which survive saponification. At room temp it is viscous (semi-solid below ~75°F); warm the bottle in hot water before measuring. Soaping temp: 100–115°F — needs warmth to pour but don't scorch the resin fraction. Strong earthy-nutty scent carries through soap. Use 5–10%; too much can mute lather. Pairs with coconut and cocoa butter in tropical-inspired bars.
oil.tucuma.name: Tucuma Butter
oil.tucuma.wiki: Rare Amazonian butter and one of the hardest plant fats — uniquely rich in lauric acid (~47%) like coconut, plus myristic (~20%), making it a butter that actually lathers. Melts ~95–105°F. Soaping temp: melt fully into oils at 110–120°F; its lauric content means it traces faster than other butters — plan your swirls accordingly. Use 5–15% for hardness AND bubbles in one ingredient. Count it toward your lauric budget alongside coconut/babassu.
oil.walnut.name: Walnut Oil
oil.walnut.wiki: High-iodine specialty oil. Allergy labeling matters if you sell. Use sparingly for novelty/conditioning; prefer more stable oils for bulk.
oil.wheat-germ.name: Wheat Germ Oil
oil.wheat-germ.wiki: Nature's antioxidant powerhouse — exceptionally high in natural vitamin E (tocopherols), which fights rancidity in the bar. Thick, amber, and unrefined with a distinctive cereal scent. As a bonus, the vitamin E can help protect other unsaturated oils in your recipe — a tiny amount goes a long way. Soaping temp: stable at normal temps (100–120°F) but don't overheat; the tocopherols degrade above ~200°F. Use 2–8% as a conditioner + natural preservative helper. Not gluten-free; label accordingly.

quality.mildness.hint: Oleic + linoleic + linolenic + ricinoleic + palmitoleic — olive, avocado, macadamia, soft oils, castor. Low can feel harsh; very high is gentle but softens the bar.

wax.beeswax.cure: Ready sooner; honey scent is the star
wax.beeswax.name: Beeswax
wax.beeswax.wick: Needs substantial wicking; pure beeswax burns hot
wax.beeswax.wiki: Natural wax with inherent honey aroma. Pure beeswax candles are often unscented or lightly scented — FO load is limited and can fight the natural smell. Hard, high-melt, long-burning. Frequently blended with coconut or soy to soften and improve throw. Food-grade vs candle-grade filtering affects color and scent.
wax.coconut-apricot.name: Coconut Apricot Wax
wax.coconut-apricot.wiki: Premium soft wax known for strong throw and smooth tops when poured correctly. Lower melt point means careful shipping in heat. Follow manufacturer FO and dye guidance; some colors migrate in very soft waxes.
wax.coconut-soy.name: Coconut-Soy Blend
wax.coconut-soy.wick: Soft pools — wick so full melt pool forms in 2–4 h
wax.coconut-soy.wiki: Creamy luxury blend with excellent scent throw for many FOs. Can be softer in warm rooms; match wick and vessel. Follow brand-specific pour and FO temps — coconut fractions vary widely between suppliers.
wax.gel.name: Gel Wax
wax.gel.wick: Special gel wicks; never treat like soy
wax.gel.wiki: Mineral-oil + resin gel. Crystal clear for embeds and novelty. ONLY gel-safe fragrances and dyes — wrong FO can cloud or create fire hazards. Higher working temps; bubble management is a skill. Not a beginner “first candle” wax. Follow supplier safety sheets strictly.
wax.palm-wax.name: Palm Wax
wax.palm-wax.wick: Crystalline structure can affect burn path — test
wax.palm-wax.wiki: Known for feathery crystalline tops when poured hot into cooler molds/jars. Hard, opaque, unique aesthetic. Sourcing ethics (RSPO) matter to many customers. Follow brand crystal-forming instructions — pour temp is everything for the look.
wax.paraffin-container.name: Paraffin (container)
wax.paraffin-container.wick: Classic CD/LX testing charts often based on paraffin
wax.paraffin-container.wiki: Petroleum-derived classic candle wax. Excellent hot throw and color pop; predictable for many wick charts. Choose container-grade melt points. Some makers blend with soy for marketing or aesthetics. Ventilate workspaces; follow FO flash-point rules when heating.
wax.paraffin-pillar.name: Paraffin (pillar)
wax.paraffin-pillar.wick: Match melt point and diameter; avoid mushrooming
wax.paraffin-pillar.wiki: Harder paraffin for freestanding forms. Lower FO % than container work. Requires good mold release and controlled cooling to reduce sinkholes — save some wax for top-offs. Core wicking must be straight and well-secured.
wax.parasoy.name: Para-Soy Blend
wax.parasoy.wick: Often easier hot throw; still test burn
wax.parasoy.wiki: Paraffin + soy hybrid aiming for soy aesthetics with paraffin throw. Popular for strong FO performance and smoother tops. Check SDS/brand FO max — some tolerate 10–12% well. Disclose blend content if you market ingredients.
wax.soy-111.cure: 1–2 weeks for full cold throw judgment
wax.soy-111.name: Soy Wax (container)
wax.soy-111.wick: Often needs hotter wick than paraffin of same diameter
wax.soy-111.wiki: Hydrogenated soybean oil wax formulated for containers. Creamy tops, clean marketing story, milder hot throw than paraffin for some fragrances. Sensitive to pour temp and FO choice — too-hot pours can cause wet spots; too-cool can rough the top. Always test your exact brand (GG464, C3, 464-clones, etc. differ).
wax.soy-pillar.name: Soy Wax (pillar/mold)
wax.soy-pillar.wick: Higher melt point — match wick to avoid tunneling
wax.soy-pillar.wiki: Higher-melt soy or soy blends meant to stand alone without a jar. Lower FO ceilings than container soy. Requires clean unmolding technique and often stearic or palm additives in commercial pillar mixes. Test diameter carefully — pillars punish under-wicking.

wiki.app-soap-ui.s0.body:
Pick g, oz, or lb with the unit tabs. Enter a dedicated Total oils weight — this is the recipe ceiling (combined oil batch size). It does not change when you type individual oils.

Each oil row has both Weight and % of total always editable:
• Type a weight → that oil’s % updates from weight ÷ Total oils. Other oils stay put.
• Type a % → that oil’s weight updates from % × Total oils. Other oils stay put.

Optional helpers: Scale weights to total (keeps ratios) and Apply % to weights. Lye/water results stay locked until oil % totals 100% and oil weights sum to the Total oils ceiling.

wiki.app-soap-ui.s1.body: Add rows for each oil/butter. Weight and % are both live against the Total oils ceiling — the app never auto-rewrites your other oils after you enter a weight. Tap the info chip on an oil (or open wiki for that oil) for encyclopedia notes. SAP used in results is NaOH or KOH depending on lye type. Custom recipe notes sit under the recipe toolbar for batch reminders, FO blend, mold, cure plan, etc.

wiki.app-units.s0.body:
Soap and candle both support grams, ounces, and pounds. Switching the unit tabs converts oil weights and the total-oils field so the recipe stays the same mass. Math is linear in whatever unit you pick — do not mix units inside one batch by hand.

Use a scale that resolves 0.1 g (or 0.01 oz) for lye. Volume cups are not accurate enough for lye or FO. When a supplier gives SAP as KOH numbers, convert or use their NaOH table - this app database is NaOH-based reference values.

wiki.candle-basics.s0.body:
Core loop: choose wax system → size wax to vessel fill weight → select wick family → melt gently → add FO at recommended temp → mix thoroughly → pour at pour temp → finish tops → cure → test burn → adjust wick/FO/pour.

Heat wax in a dedicated melter or double boiler with a thermometer. Never leave melting wax unattended. Keep FO away from open flame; know flash points.

wiki.candle-fragrance-load.s0.body:
Fragrance load is FO weight ÷ wax weight × 100. Cold throw = scent of unlit candle; hot throw = scent while burning. Excess FO can sweat, clog wicks, soot, or violate IFRA.

Stay inside your wax brand’s tested max and the FO supplier’s candle category limit (use the lower of the two). Cure time matters — soy especially needs days to weeks before you judge throw. Mix FO long enough (often ~2 minutes) for even binding.

Label basics people actually read: never leave burning candle unattended; keep away from kids/pets/drafts/curtains; trim wick; don’t burn to the extreme bottom; max burn session (e.g. 4 hours); surface must be heat-safe.

As a maker: document batch codes, FO lot numbers, and test results. Glass can fail from thermal shock — quality vessels matter.

wiki.candle-vessels-tops.s0.body:
Wet spots (soy glass adhesion): temperature, glass prep, and expectations — often cosmetic.
Frosting (soy crystal bloom): natural for many soy lines; texture or color choices hide it.
Sinkholes / craters: pour temp, cool rate; poke relief holes and top-off pours while warm.
Jump lines: pour hotter or insulated cool.

Weigh wax for fill height rather than trusting jar “oz” labels — fluid oz ≠ wax weight oz. Vessel presets in the app use approximate fill weights.

wiki.candle-wicking.s0.body:
Wick size depends on wax blend, FO (some make flames lazy), colorants, vessel diameter and shape, and ambient conditions. App hints by diameter are starting points for ECO/CD-like families — not prescriptions.

Test burn: trim to ~¼", burn on level surface, aim for full melt pool to the edge in ~2–4 hours for many containers without a raging flame. Tunneling → hotter wick or correct FO/wax. Mushrooming/sooting → smaller wick, FO issues, or drafts.

Wide vessels often need dual or triple wicks rather than one huge wick.

wiki.oils-butters.s0.body:
Shea: conditioning, creamy, can slow trace and add “slime” lather in a good way; often 5–20%. Unrefined has scent/color.
Cocoa: hardness + snappy bar, chocolate aroma if unrefined; 5–15% common. Helps palm-free hardness.
Mango: between shea and cocoa for many soapers; elegant skin feel.

Butters can seize with some FRs and need full melt. Too much butter without enough bubbly oils makes a hard but weak-lather bar.

wiki.oils-castor-jojoba.s0.body:
Castor (ricinoleic) boosts fluffy lather and humectant feel — 2–8% is the sweet spot; higher gets sticky.
Jojoba is a liquid wax ester, low SAP, luxurious; expensive — often 1–5% or in superfats.
Neem: medicinal reputation, strong odor; low %.
Meadowfoam: stable, silky, premium.
Beeswax: hardens and adds drag; low SAP; 1–3% typical or bars feel waxy.
Argan/macadamia/apricot: conditioning accents in the soft-oil slot.

wiki.oils-lauric.s0.body:
Coconut, palm kernel, babassu, and fractionated coconut sit in the lauric camp. They saponify to very hard, white, high-lather soap. Skin strip risk rises as their combined % climbs — especially with low superfat.

Guidelines many soapers use: keep combined lauric oils near or under ~30% for face/body bars; higher for laundry, shaving with care, or salt bars with generous superfat. Fractionated coconut has a very high SAP — weigh meticulously.

wiki.oils-lauric.title: Lauric oils: coconut family
wiki.oils-overview.s0.body:
Every oil in the calculator has SAP (NaOH), optional iodine & INS, category, suggested max %, hardness/conditioning/lather tags, and a wiki blurb. Open any oil article from this category list or search by name (olive, shea, castor…).

Fatty-acid intuition:
• Lauric/myristic (coconut, palm kernel, babassu) — hard, bubbly, cleansing
• Palmitic/stearic (palm, tallow, cocoa) — hard, stable, creamy
• Oleic (olive, avocado, high-oleic oils) — conditioning, slower trace
• Linoleic/linolenic (grapeseed, hemp, safflower) — silky, softer, higher rancidity risk
wiki.oils-overview.s1.body: Many teaching recipes look like: 25–40% soft conditioning oil, 20–30% hard bubbly (coconut family), 20–30% hard creamy (palm/tallow/butter), 5% castor for bubbles. Adjust for climate, scent, and skin goals.

1. Switch to Candle mode.
2. Choose Soy Wax (container) or your brand’s closest profile.

6. Melt wax, cool to FO temp per brand, stir FO 2 minutes, pour, wick centered.
7. Cure days before judging cold throw (soy often 1–2 weeks).

wiki.quick-start-soap.s0.body:
1. Stay on Soap mode.
2. Load the Everyday Bar preset (olive / coconut / palm / castor).
3. Set total oils to the size you want (scale all amounts, or use Scale batch).
4. Superfat 5%, water ~33% of oils (or lye concentration 33%).
5. Fragrance 3% of oils for most soap FOs (check IFRA).
6. Read NaOH needed — weigh carefully.
7. Save recipe with a name you’ll recognize later.
wiki.quick-start-soap.s1.body: Suit up (goggles, gloves, long sleeves). Weigh water into a heat-safe pitcher. Weigh lye separately. Add lye to water outdoors or under ventilation — never water into lye. Cool lye solution and oils to roughly 100–120°F (recipe-dependent). Combine, stick-blend to trace, add FO/color, pour mold, insulate or CPOP as preferred, unmold, cut, cure 4–6 weeks.

wiki.ref-formulas.s0.body:
Soap pure lye (NaOH) = Σ (oil_weight × sap_naoh)
Soap pure lye (KOH) = Σ (oil_weight × sap_naoh × 1.4027 ÷ 0.9)   — 1.4027 = NaOH→KOH molecular-weight ratio; ÷0.9 = 90% commercial KOH purity
Lye with superfat = pure_lye × (1 − superfat%/100) + citric_comp
Citric compensation = citric_weight × 0.624 (NaOH) or × 0.978 (90% KOH)
Water (% oils) = total_oils × (water%/100)
Water (concentration c) = lye_with_sf × (1−c)/c
Water (discount d) = total_oils × 0.38 × (1−d/100)
Soap FO = total_oils × (fo%/100)

Candle FO = total_wax × (fo%/100)
Dye blocks ≈ (wax_lb) × (blocks_per_lb)

Weighted iodine/INS = weight-average of oils that have values.

wiki.ref-troubleshooting-candle.s0.body:
Weak hot throw — cure longer, wick up carefully, FO quality/load, vessel diameter, room size.
Soot / huge flame — wick down, trim, drafts, FO overload.
Sweating FO — load too high for wax, temp swing storage, FO compatibility.
Sinkholes — top-off, pour temp, wick poke while setting.
Crack tops — cool slower, pour temp, or gentle warm room.
Wick drowns — wick too small or FO clogging; try different wick series.

wiki.ref-troubleshooting-soap.s0.body:
Seize / rice / apple sauce — FO reaction, temp, or over-blending; work fast or switch FO; soap on.
Separation — incomplete emulsion; stick blend more; worst cases may need rebatch.
Soft bar after cure — high soft oils, high SF, high water, humid cure; reformulate harder, longer cure.
Grabby / lye-heavy feel — weighing error or bad SAP; do not use on skin; rebatch with care or discard safely.
DOS — high unsaturation, metals, heat/light; add ROE next time, store cool, check oils.
 partial gel / glycerin rivers — thermal; cosmetic or adjust insulation.

wiki.safety-candle-shop.s0.body:
Wax fires: never quench with water — it can splatter burning wax. Lid/smother and call emergency services if needed. Keep a rated extinguisher.

Thermostat control beats “guess the microwave.” FO is flammable — add off direct flame, know flash points, ventilate strong scents. Dye and FO staining is real; protect surfaces.

Ergonomics: repetitive pouring and heavy pour pots — plan lifts. Label everything that isn’t water.
wiki.safety-candle-shop.title: Candle studio safety
wiki.safety-lye.s0.body:
Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide cause severe chemical burns and eye damage. Work like a chemist on purpose.

• PPE: side-shield goggles or face shield, gloves, long sleeves, closed shoes; apron smart.
• Always add lye to water — never water to lye (volcanic splash risk).
• Mix in heat-safe, lye-safe containers (HDPE, stainless, etc. — know your plastic).
• Fumes on mixing: ventilate; don’t bend your face over the pitcher.
• Vinegar is not a first-aid magic wash for eyes — flush with water and seek medical help. Weak acid neutralization on skin is debated; priority is copious water and medical care for serious exposure.
• Store lye locked, labeled, dry, away from aluminum and kids/pets.
• Clean tools dedicated to soap; keep food separate.
wiki.safety-lye.title: Lye safety (NaOH / KOH)
wiki.safety-process.s0.body:
Clear the space of kids, pets, and clutter. No drinking cups that look like lye water. Label pitchers. Keep paper towels and a plan for spills (contain, then careful cleanup with PPE).

Fresh soap batter is still caustic until saponification advances — treat molded soap with respect for 24–48+ hours. Zap test / pH habits vary by maker; uncured bars are not mild facial cleansers.

Dispose of lye water per local hazardous guidance — not casually down storm drains.

wiki.soap-additives.s0.body: Additives are everything you put in the batch beyond oils, lye, water, and fragrance: exfoliants, clays, milks, sugars, salts, botanicals, colorants, and shelf-life helpers. Usage rates are quoted as a percentage of total oil weight (the same base as fragrance). The calculator flags anything below or above the recommended range so you can see where a recipe sits at a glance.
wiki.soap-additives.s1.body: Each additive in the catalog lists a typical % of oils (e.g. kaolin 0.5–3%), a bench-side spoon measure per pound of oils (PPO), when to add it, what it does, and cautions. Enter an amount by weight (g/oz/lb) or by spoon (tsp/tbsp); the row shows the PPO guidance, phase, live % of oils, and whether you are inside the range. Spoon weights are approximate — powders pack differently, so weigh when precision matters.
wiki.soap-additives.s1.heading: Reading the additive table
wiki.soap-additives.s10.body:
• Weigh additives, don’t guess scoops.
• Add at light trace so the batter is fluid enough to mix evenly.
• Powders (clays, charcoal, TiO₂) should be dispersed in a little oil or water first to avoid clumps.
• Anything that heats the batch (honey, sugar, milks) needs a cooler lye solution and a watchful eye.
• More is not better — staying inside the range keeps lather, hardness, and skin feel intact.
wiki.soap-additives.s10.heading: Rules of thumb
wiki.soap-additives.s2.body: Colloidal (finely ground) oatmeal is the gentlest scrub — beta-glucan calms itchy, dry, sensitive skin. Use 1–4% of oils and grind it to a powder or the bar feels scratchy. Above ~5% the bar softens and trace thickens. Sprinkle a little on top of the loaf for a decorative finish with zero scratchiness.
wiki.soap-additives.s2.heading: Exfoliants: ground oats
wiki.soap-additives.s3.body: Kaolin (0.5–3%): silky slip, gentle, brightens color. Bentonite (0.5–3%): strong draw-out, creamier lather, can be drying. French green / illite and rhassoul: spa-style detox with natural tint. All clays absorb water and thicken batter — disperse in a little oil or water first and add at light trace. Keep rates modest or the bar can become drying and mute lather.
wiki.soap-additives.s3.heading: Clays
wiki.soap-additives.s4.body: Honey (0.5–5%): humectant + extra bubbles, but it heats the batch — start at 1 tsp PPO and watch for gel or overheat. Sugar (0.5–2%): dissolved in the water phase, boosts lather in high-oleic bars. Sodium lactate (1–3%): hardens the bar and speeds unmolding — add to cooled lye solution.
wiki.soap-additives.s4.heading: Liquids & sugars
wiki.soap-additives.s5.body: Goat milk powder (2–5%) and other milks make creamy, gentle bars. Keep the lye solution cool — hot milk + lye scorches orange or brown. Dissolve powder in water before the lye, or add at trace. The lactic acid in milk is naturally mild on skin.
wiki.soap-additives.s5.heading: Milks
wiki.soap-additives.s6.body: Salt (1–4%): harder bar, dense creamy lather; dissolve in the water phase first. True salt bars are 25–50%+ salt with ~20% superfat — a different style than this gentle range. Silk (tussah, a pinch per pound dissolved in lye water) adds a silky glide and strengthens the bar.
wiki.soap-additives.s6.heading: Salts & silk
wiki.soap-additives.s7.body: Citric acid (0.5–2% of oils) chelates hard-water minerals so the soap lathers rich instead of scummy. It also neutralizes lye: every 1 g of citric acid consumes ~0.624 g NaOH (0.88 g pure KOH ≈ 0.98 g of 90% KOH). This calculator adds the compensating lye automatically and tells you the adjusted amount. Never drop citric acid into lye solution — dissolve it in the water first, then add the lye.
wiki.soap-additives.s7.heading: Citric acid & lye math
wiki.soap-additives.s8.body: Activated charcoal (0.3–1.5%): true black, sift into oil first. Titanium dioxide (0.2–1%): bright white base, disperse in oil not water. Skin-safe mica (0.1–1%): shimmer and color — never craft-store mica. Spirulina and French green clay give natural greens that can shift in lye; test small batches. Light botanicals (lavender buds, rose petals) are decorative — sprinkle on top so they stay pretty.
wiki.soap-additives.s8.heading: Colorants & botanicals
wiki.soap-additives.s9.body: Rosemary oleoresin (ROE, 0.05–0.5%) is a natural antioxidant that slows rancidity (DOS) — a few drops per pound of oils is plenty, added to the warm oils or at trace.
wiki.soap-additives.s9.heading: Shelf life helpers

wiki.soap-cure.s0.body:
Cure is mostly water loss plus crystalline finishing of the soap matrix. Bars usually need 4–6 weeks (castile much longer) in airy, dry, indirect light conditions, flipped occasionally.

Gel phase (through the middle) can deepen colors; force gel with light heat or prevent with chill for swirl clarity — both valid.

Soda ash is sodium carbonate on the surface from CO₂ — cosmetic. Steam, spritz alcohol early, or plan a plane/wash. Not the same as lye-heavy soap (which feels grabby and fails zap/pH checks).
wiki.soap-cure.title: Cure, hardness & soda ash
wiki.soap-fatty-acids.s0.body:
• Lauric (12:0) — coconut, palm kernel, babassu. Rock-hard bar, big fluffy bubbles, strong cleansing. Overdo it and the bar strips skin: keep total lauric oils moderate (~15–30%) or superfat higher.
• Myristic (14:0) — coconut, palm kernel. Hardness, cleansing, and lather with a slightly milder edge than lauric.
• Palmitic (16:0) — palm, tallow, lard, cocoa. The workhorse: hardness, creamy stable lather, longevity.
• Stearic (18:0) — cocoa, tallow, shea. Hardness and creamy lather with the silkiest feel of the saturates; contributes most per % to bar firmness.
• Oleic (18:1) — olive, avocado, canola, high-oleic sunflower. Conditioning and mildness; slow trace; softer, longer-cure bars at high %.
• Linoleic (18:2) — sunflower, safflower, grapeseed, rice bran. Conditioning but the first to go rancid; keep moderate for shelf life.
• Linolenic (18:3) — flax, hemp, chia, some camelina. Very conditioning, very prone to DOS — use small %.
• Ricinoleic (18:1 OH) — castor. The oddball: boosts bubbles AND creaminess AND conditioning; humectant. 3–8% is the sweet spot.
• Palmitoleic (16:1) — macadamia, some sea buckthorn. Minor; adds a bit of conditioning.
wiki.soap-fatty-acids.s0.heading: The cast
wiki.soap-fatty-acids.s1.body: Saturates (lauric → stearic) build the bar: hardness, lather, longevity. Unsaturates (oleic → linolenic) build the feel: conditioning, mildness. A typical balanced bar is roughly 40% saturated / 60% unsaturated. When a recipe feels off, look at the quality profile: too soft → add palmitic/stearic (palm, tallow, lard, butters); no bubbles → add lauric (coconut); drying → cut lauric and raise superfat or add oleic; short shelf life → reduce linoleic/linolenic oils and use antioxidants.

wiki.soap-fragrance.s0.body:
Soap FO is usually calculated as % of total oil weight. Many soapers land 3–6% depending on FO strength and IFRA category limits for leave-on vs rinse-off. Essential oils can need lower rates and have phototoxicity or sensitization limits (citrus folds, cinnamon, etc.).

PPD (parts per diem / dermal limits) and IFRA categories are legal/safety frameworks from FO suppliers — always read the document for that SKU. Some FOs ricing, accelerate, or discolor (vanillin → brown). Test small.

wiki.soap-iodine-ins.s0.body:
Iodine value estimates unsaturation — higher iodine tends toward softer bars and faster oxidation (DOS risk). Very high blend iodine (>70-ish weighted) is a yellow flag for shelf life; balance with hard fats and antioxidants (rosemary oleoresin, careful storage).

INS (iodine to SAP number style index) is a traditional soaper heuristic for hardness/conditioning balance. Many aim roughly 136–165 for bar feel, but excellent soaps exist outside that band. Use as a compass, not a law.
wiki.soap-iodine-ins.s0.heading: Iodine value
wiki.soap-iodine-ins.s1.body: INS = SAP value − iodine value (a classic industry shortcut: saponification minus unsaturation). It is a hardness/stability proxy: high INS (coconut ~258, palm kernel ~227) = hard, stable, but potentially drying; low INS (castor ~95, olive ~109) = soft, conditioning. The common balanced range is roughly 136–165. INS is a rough guide, not a law — treat it as one more vote in the quality profile.

wiki.soap-liquid.s0.body:
Liquid soap uses potassium hydroxide. This app computes KOH from NaOH SAP × 1.4027 (molecular-weight ratio), then ÷ 0.9 for the ~90% purity of commercial KOH flakes. Process is often hot-process to a paste, neutralized (e.g. slight boric or citric solutions per your method), then diluted with distilled water to a usable viscosity.

Superfat in liquid soap is handled carefully — excess oils can cloud or separate. Dilution ratios vary (often paste:water around 1:1 to 1:2 by weight as a starting experiment). Preservatives may be needed once water activity and use pattern demand them — research modern liquid soap preservation; this wiki is not a micro lab.

wiki.soap-liquid.title: Liquid soap (KOH) basics
wiki.soap-palm-free.s0.body:
Palm brings palmitic hardness and creamy bubbles. Palm-free builders often use: tallow or lard, cocoa/mango butters, stearic acid (careful usage), higher rice bran/olive with longer cure, or commercial palm-free hard oil blends.

Expect reformulation — simply deleting palm and redistributing % usually softens the bar. Watch iodine and cure time. Babassu or coconut can restore some bubbles but increase dryness if pushed too high.

wiki.soap-quality.s0.body:
Below the batch results you get seven quality numbers, each with an ideal range (same targets used by the classic SoapCalc). Each is the combined % of the fatty acids that drive it — a higher contributing fatty acid moves the bar toward that quality.

• Hardness (29–54): lauric + myristic + palmitic + stearic. Below ~29 the bar dents and dissolves fast; above ~54 it is rock-hard and slow to wear (can get brittle to cut).
• Cleansing (12–22): lauric + myristic (coconut family). Above ~22 strips skin oils; below ~12 can feel under-cleaning.
• Conditioning (44–69): oleic + linoleic + linolenic + ricinoleic. Above ~69 the bar softens and cures slower.
• Bubbly lather (14–46): lauric + myristic — fluffy suds. Too high with low superfat = drying.
• Creamy lather (16–48): palmitic + stearic + ricinoleic — dense, lotion-like suds.
• Longevity (18–47): palmitic + stearic — how slowly the bar wears down.
• Mildness (40–70): oleic + linoleic + linolenic + ricinoleic — gentle skin feel (low is harsh).
wiki.soap-quality.s0.heading: The seven qualities
wiki.soap-quality.s1.body: The green band is the balanced-bar target. A marker inside the band means that quality is in range; outside means low (amber) or high (red) with a one-line hint on what to adjust. No recipe is perfect on all seven at once — castile is conditioning but soft, high-coconut is hard and bubbly but harsh. Aim for everything inside the band for an everyday bar, then break rules deliberately (salt bars, facial bars, laundry). Iodine and INS sit in the results meta row: iodine 41–70 keeps shelf life sane; INS 136–165 tracks hardness/stability. The saturated:unsaturated ratio under the bars typically lands near 40:60 for a balanced bar.
wiki.soap-quality.s1.heading: How to use it
wiki.soap-quality.s2.body: Each oil has a fatty-acid profile (see its oil article). The calculator weights those profiles by your oil amounts, so a quality value is simply the sum of the contributing fatty acids in your recipe. Values are guidance from craft averages — real bars vary with cure, water, superfat, and additives.
wiki.soap-quality.s2.heading: Where the numbers come from

wiki.soap-saponification.s0.body: Saponification is the chemical reaction between triglycerides (oils/fats) and a strong alkali (NaOH or KOH). Each oil needs a characteristic amount of lye to convert fully — that ratio is the SAP value. This calculator multiplies each oil’s weight by its NaOH SAP (or × 1.4027 ÷ 0.9 for 90%-pure KOH), sums them, then reduces by your superfat %.
wiki.soap-saponification.s1.body: Natural oils vary by cultivar, season, and refining. Published SAP values are averages. Serious makers verify with supplier COAs or titrate. Treat app numbers as planning defaults, not lab certificates.
wiki.soap-saponification.s1.heading: Why SAP tables differ
wiki.soap-saponification.title: Saponification explained
wiki.soap-superfat.s0.body:
Superfat (lye discount) deliberately underdoses lye so a percentage of oils remain unsaponified. Benefits: insurance against measurement error, milder skin feel, room for luxurious butters. Costs: too much softens bars, can invite DOS (dreaded orange spots) or shorter shelf life, and greasy feel.

Common ranges:
• Everyday bars: 4–6%
• High-coconut/salt bars: 8–15%+
• Liquid soap: often cooked to neutrality then diluted; superfat strategy differs
• Laundry soap: sometimes 0–2%
wiki.soap-superfat.title: Superfat & lye discount
wiki.soap-trace.s0.body:
Trace is when oils and lye emulsion thicken enough that drizzled batter leaves a brief mark. Light trace pours and swirls; thick trace molds texture and drops.

Speed up: stick blender pulses, heat, sugars (honey, milk solids), some FOs, high lauric oils.
Slow down: cool temps, hand stir, high olive/rice bran, some floral FOs that accelerate — know your FO.

Add clays, activated charcoal, and most powders at light trace. Stick-blend titanium dioxide carefully to avoid clumps. Always check FO and essential oil vendor acceleration notes.
wiki.soap-trace.title: Trace, temperature & additives
wiki.soap-water.s0.body: Water does not become soap — it is the reaction medium and evaporates during cure. More water = thinner batter, slower trace, longer cure to hard bar. Less water (higher lye concentration or discount) = thicker faster, risk of false trace with hard fats, shorter cure, sometimes soda ash tradeoffs.
wiki.soap-water.s1.body:
• Beginners: 33–38% water as % of oils, or ~33% lye concentration.
• Advanced swirls needing time: slightly more water, cooler temps, slow oils.
• Fast movers (milk, sugar, high coconut): consider full water and low temps.
• HP / fluid liquid soap: different water math after cook.

wiki.waxes-cure.s0.body:
Rough cure before final judgment:
• Many paraffins / para-soy: 3–7 days
• Soy & coconut-soy: 7–14 days (some FOs longer)
• Beeswax: evaluate early for burn; scent is subtle
• Gel: per brand, often shorter cosmetic set, still test burn

wiki.waxes-overview.s0.body:
Soy — plant marketing, creamy, often milder throw, frosting/wet spots common, wick carefully.
Paraffin — strong throw, predictable, various melt points for container vs pillar.
Para-soy / coconut blends — aim for hybrid performance; follow that brand’s FO max.
Beeswax — high melt, honey scent, low FO ceiling, excellent pillars/tapers.
Palm wax — crystalline tops, ethical sourcing questions, unique aesthetic.
Gel — mineral oil polymer; gel-safe FO only; different wick and safety profile.
